title: English Vocabulary in Use — Upper-intermediate (4th Edition) · Units 03–04
description: Curated dictionary-use strategies, grammatical word patterns, meaning inference, word formation and B2 contextual vocabulary.
sourceNotice: Prepared from the user-supplied book for personal study. Vocabulary targets follow source topics and exercise vocabulary; all teaching examples and notes are newly written, and original exercises, extended passages and illustrations are not reproduced.

audit.scope: Teaching sections, illustrations, diagrams, exercises and relevant answer-key entries checked for lexical and grammatical coverage.
audit.pronunciation: Broad British IPA for checked words and some short expressions; where confidence is insufficient, IPA is omitted rather than guessed. IPA does not exhaustively represent accent variants or connected speech.
audit.languagePolicy: All content is in English except Portuguese translations under pt.
audit.reviewMethod: Original textbook study pages, diagrams, exercises and answer key checked; lexical and contextual review; phonetic spot-checks against Cambridge Dictionary; schema, IDs, language fields and audio-target checks. Browser speech recognition is not tested in this environment.
audit.limitations: No bundled audio files. TTS and voice-recognition quality depend on browser, selected voice and accent; no live UI import test was performed.

units.title: Unit 03 — Using your dictionary
units.source: English Vocabulary in Use — Upper-intermediate (4th Edition); printed pages 12–13 (PDF pages 13–14).
units.bookTitle: English Vocabulary in Use — Upper-intermediate (4th Edition)
learningObjectives: Use dictionary entries to check pronunciation, word stress, meaning and grammatical patterns.
Compare synonyms, antonyms, collocations, transitivity and countability.
Differentiate near synonyms and recognise that some adjectives describe people, things or both.
Practise dictionary conventions, noun–verb stress shifts and the patterns used with supply and deny.

sectionsChecked: A: What a good dictionary tells you: the basics

items.example: I use a learner's dictionary to check common patterns.
items.note: This type of dictionary includes usage information for language learners.

items.example: This dictionary includes the British pronunciation of each word.
items.note: Pronunciation includes sounds and patterns of stress.

items.example: She learned to read phonemic symbols before the course.
items.note: A written symbol representing a distinctive speech sound; dictionaries commonly use IPA.

items.example: The word stress moves in some noun–verb pairs.
items.note: The syllable given greater prominence in a word.

items.example: Mark the stressed syllable in each new word.
items.note: Notice stress placement, not merely the written spelling.

items.example: The entry explains the formal and informal usage of the expression.
items.note: In a dictionary, usage covers contexts and grammatical restrictions.

items.example: I checked the grammatical pattern before using the verb.
items.note: A recurring structure that a word normally requires.

items.example: I suggest that we postpone the meeting.
items.note: Suggest normally takes a noun, an -ing form or a that-clause, not suggest someone to do something.

items.example: She suggested taking a shorter route.
items.note: Correct: suggest doing something; not suggest to do something.

items.pt: sugerir que alguém faça alguma coisa
items.example: The consultant suggested that we review the figures.
items.note: Also possible: suggest that someone should do something. The verb following suggest is not normally a to-infinitive.

items.example: The verb expect is often followed by a to-infinitive.
items.note: The base form of a verb, sometimes preceded by to.

items.example: The sentence contains a main clause and a subordinate clause.
items.note: A unit of grammar that typically contains a subject and a verb.

items.example: The dictionary shows the word class beside each headword.
items.note: A category such as noun, verb, adjective or adverb.

items.example: Huge and enormous are near synonyms in many contexts.
items.note: Words with the same or very similar meanings; not necessarily interchangeable everywhere.

items.example: The antonym of generous is often stingy.
items.note: A word with an opposite meaning.

items.pt: perder temporariamente; colocar em algum lugar e esquecer
items.example: I often mislay my glasses when I am tired.
items.note: Usually means temporarily being unable to find an item; similar to misplace.

items.pt: guardar no lugar errado; perder temporariamente
items.example: I had misplaced the receipt, but I found it this morning.
items.note: Put something somewhere and then forget where; close to mislay.

items.example: The two former foes eventually signed a peace agreement.
items.note: A relatively literary or formal alternative to enemy.

items.example: Make a decision is a common English collocation.
items.note: Natural combinations of words commonly found together.

items.example: The organisation made a firm commitment to accessibility.
items.note: Firm expresses a strong, definite commitment.

items.example: Keep a firm grip on the handle while you climb.
items.note: A secure hold on something physical.

items.pt: alguém que acredita firmemente em algo
items.example: She is a firm believer in regular exercise.
items.note: Usually firm believer in something; expresses a strong conviction.

items.example: The verb catch is transitive in this sentence.
items.note: Normally requires a direct object in the use being described.

items.example: Arrive is generally an intransitive verb.
items.note: Does not take a direct object in the use being described.

items.example: He caught the ball before it hit the ground.
items.note: In this sense, catch takes a direct object: catch something.

items.example: Everyone laughed when the lights suddenly went out.
items.note: Intransitive in this use; laugh at someone or something is a separate prepositional pattern.

items.pt: magoante; ofensivo; que causa dor emocional
items.example: His hurtful comment made the discussion difficult.
items.note: Can describe a person, remark or action that causes emotional pain.

items.example: I wish you had not made such a hurtful remark.
items.note: Common pairing with hurtful for something said.

items.example: Chair is a countable noun, so we can say three chairs.
items.note: Can normally be used with a number and has a plural form.

items.example: Furniture is an uncountable noun in English.
items.note: Not normally used with a/an or a regular plural in the relevant sense.

items.pt: tesauro visual; mapa visual de sinônimos
items.example: A visual thesaurus helps me compare near synonyms.
items.note: A diagram or tool showing networks of related words.

items.example: A network of meaning links words with related ideas.
items.note: Related terms can be organised by semantic similarity, not just translation.

items.example: I found the lecture on neuroscience fascinating.
items.note: Something that holds a person's attention strongly.

items.example: We stayed in an enchanting village in the mountains.
items.note: Often conveys charm or a magical quality.

items.example: The documentary was enthralling from beginning to end.
items.note: So interesting that it holds your full attention.

items.example: The speaker told a captivating story about her research.
items.note: Holds your interest or attention through appeal or charm.

items.example: The dancer gave an entrancing performance.
items.note: So beautiful or interesting that you become absorbed.

items.example: The music had a bewitching quality.
items.note: Suggests unusual charm or spell-like attraction; somewhat literary.

items.example: It was an absorbing account of a scientific discovery.
items.note: Requires and holds close attention; often used for books and activities.

items.pt: eletrizante; que prende completamente a atenção
items.example: The witness gave a riveting account of the rescue.
items.note: Extremely exciting or compelling.

items.example: She spent the evening reading an engrossing novel.
items.note: Holds your attention so fully that you notice little else.

items.example: The series ended with a gripping final episode.
items.note: Especially compelling or tense; often used for stories or drama.

items.example: Education plays an important role in social mobility.
items.note: The final syllable sequence is pronounced with /ʃən/.

items.example: Check that your passport is valid before you travel.
items.note: The stress falls on the first syllable.

items.example: The fence was leaning towards the road.
items.note: Pronounced with a long /iː/ sound at the start.

items.example: Freedom of expression is a fundamental civil liberty.
items.note: The first syllable is stressed in British pronunciation.

items.example: I have planned two hours of revision for the exam.
items.note: In British English, revision also means studying before an examination.

items.example: Her brother works as a software engineer.
items.note: Note /ð/, the voiced th sound.

items.example: Each device has a unique serial number.
items.note: Stress falls on the final syllable.

items.example: We found an elegant solution to the problem.
items.note: Stress falls on the first syllable.

items.example: The patient needs to be seen urgently.
items.note: The main stress is on the first syllable.

items.example: He raised an eyebrow when he heard the news.
items.note: Main stress falls on the first part of the compound.

items.example: Please record the temperature every five minutes.
items.note: Verb: stress on the second syllable; compare the noun record /ˈrekɔːd/.

items.example: The thermometer showed a higher temperature today.
items.note: Stress on the second syllable in British English.

items.example: We read an extract from the novel in class.
items.note: Noun: first-syllable stress; the verb extract has stress on the second syllable.

items.example: Regular exercise can be part of a healthy lifestyle.
items.note: The main stress falls at the beginning of the compound.

items.example: The factory supplies components to several manufacturers.
items.note: Supply something to someone or supply someone with something.

items.example: The farm supplies vegetables to nearby restaurants.
items.note: Correct: supply goods to a recipient; not supply goods at someone.

items.example: The company supplied the technicians with protective gloves.
items.note: The recipient is the direct object in this pattern.

items.example: The manager denied the allegations.
items.note: For denying an action, use deny doing something or deny that a clause is true.

items.example: She denied sharing the confidential file.
items.note: Deny is followed by an -ing form, not a to-infinitive in this use.

items.example: The director denied that any records had been deleted.
items.note: A that-clause is an alternative to deny doing something.

items.example: The newspaper published an allegation of corruption.
items.note: A claim that someone has done something wrong, not necessarily proven.

items.example: It was a sad day for the whole team.
items.note: Can describe a person or a situation, event or story.

items.example: We were lucky to catch the last train.
items.note: Can describe a person or a fortunate event or outcome.

items.example: She seems content with her new job.
items.note: Adjective, stressed on the second syllable; usually describes a person who is satisfied.

items.example: The walls felt damp after several days of rain.
items.note: Commonly describes things or conditions, not people's personalities.

items.example: There was an awkward silence after the question.
items.note: May describe people, social situations, movements or objects that are hard to use.

items.example: Attendance is compulsory for all new employees.
items.note: Typically describes rules, activities or requirements rather than a person's character.

items.example: They is a pronoun that can refer to one person.
items.note: Often abbreviated pron in dictionaries.

items.example: Although is a conjunction that introduces a contrast.
items.note: Often abbreviated conj in dictionaries.

items.example: In is a preposition in the phrase in the room.
items.note: Often abbreviated prep in dictionaries.

items.example: Carefully is an adverb describing how something is done.
items.note: Often abbreviated adv in dictionaries.

items.example: Colour is the usual spelling in British English.
items.note: UK labels mark British usage; forms may differ elsewhere.

items.example: The word idea is countable.
items.note: The dictionary label noun [C] means a countable noun.

items.example: The word advice is uncountable.
items.note: The dictionary label noun [U] means an uncountable noun.

units.title: Unit 04 — Guessing and explaining meaning
units.source: English Vocabulary in Use — Upper-intermediate (4th Edition); printed pages 14–15 (PDF pages 15–16).
units.bookTitle: English Vocabulary in Use — Upper-intermediate (4th Edition)
learningObjectives: Infer the meanings of unfamiliar words from visual, situational, lexical and grammatical clues.
Use compounds, word structure and similarities across languages while avoiding false friends.
Explain probable meanings using natural expressions of similarity, category, purpose and uncertainty.
Apply inference strategies to animal descriptions, physical objects, figurative expressions and affixes.

sectionsChecked: A: Working out meaning from context

items.example: Try to work out the meaning before looking it up.
items.note: Work out means solve or discover through reasoning in this context.

items.example: The context makes the unfamiliar phrase easier to understand.
items.note: Words or circumstances surrounding an expression.

items.example: A contextual clue helped me understand the technical term.
items.note: An indication from surrounding information; the source describes several types of clues.

items.example: Underline unfamiliar words while you read.
items.note: Something you do not know or recognise.

items.example: The drawing provided a useful visual clue.
items.note: An image or visible detail that suggests a meaning.

items.example: The report included film footage of the storm.
items.note: Recorded moving images used in reports or documentaries.

items.example: I first heard the expression during a news broadcast.
items.note: A television, radio or online news programme.

items.example: Her background knowledge made the article easier to follow.
items.note: Information you already know about a topic or situation.

items.example: The earthquake damaged several buildings near the coast.
items.note: A sudden movement of the Earth's surface.

items.example: She planted a gladiolus beside the garden path.
items.note: The flower's meaning can be inferred from its gardening context.

items.example: He placed the flowers in a tall glass vase.
items.note: A container used to display cut flowers.

items.example: A grammatical clue showed that the missing word was an adjective.
items.note: The position of a word and its surrounding grammar can indicate its class.

items.example: Some people are superstitious about the number thirteen.
items.note: Describes someone who believes that particular signs or actions bring good or bad luck.

items.example: He stepped gingerly onto the icy pavement.
items.note: An adverb meaning cautiously, especially to avoid injury or damage.

items.section: B · Word structure and related languages
items.example: Headscarf is a compound word made from two familiar words.
items.note: A word formed by combining two or more elements.

items.section: B · Word structure and related languages
items.example: She wore a bright headscarf on the cold morning.
items.note: A scarf worn on the head; understanding the parts helps reveal the whole meaning.

items.section: B · Word structure and related languages
items.example: The prefix un- often creates a negative meaning.
items.note: An element added before a word or base.

items.section: B · Word structure and related languages
items.example: The suffix -ness can form a noun from an adjective.
items.note: An element added after a word or base.

items.section: B · Word structure and related languages
items.example: Understanding word formation helps with unfamiliar terms.
items.note: The process of making new words using roots, prefixes, suffixes or compounds.

items.section: B · Word structure and related languages
items.example: Knowing the word root can help with scientific vocabulary.
items.note: A basic word element from which other words develop.

items.section: B · Word structure and related languages
items.example: I noticed a similarity between the two terms.
items.note: Shared characteristics that make words or concepts look alike.

items.section: B · Word structure and related languages
items.example: Several medical terms are of Latin origin.
items.note: Origin identifies the language a word historically comes from.

items.section: B · Word structure and related languages
items.example: Many everyday English words are of Germanic origin.
items.note: English contains vocabulary from several historical language families.

items.section: B · Word structure and related languages
items.example: Actual is a false friend for Portuguese speakers who expect atual.
items.note: A word resembling one in another language but having a different meaning.

items.section: B · Word structure and related languages
items.example: She bought a thoughtful gift for her colleague.
items.note: English gift means present; the same spelling means poison in German.

items.example: A sundial is a kind of clock that uses shadows.
items.note: A useful phrase to put an unfamiliar item into a broader category.

items.example: A shuttle is something like a small bus.
items.note: Helps explain approximate similarities without claiming two things are identical.

items.example: A whisk is something you use for mixing ingredients.
items.note: Use for followed by an -ing verb to state the purpose of an object.

items.example: In this context, the verb could mean remove.
items.note: Expresses a tentative explanation of meaning.

items.example: Given the context, the phrase must mean almost finished.
items.note: Must conveys a strong inference, rather than an obligation, in this use.

items.example: A tortoise moved slowly across the dry grass.
items.note: A mostly land-dwelling reptile; the Brazilian term jabuti is more specific than the broad English category.

items.example: The museum displayed several shelled creatures.
items.note: Having a hard protective covering called a shell.

items.example: A snake is a reptile, not a mammal.
items.note: A cold-blooded vertebrate such as a snake or lizard.

items.example: The region is famed for its traditional cuisine.
items.note: Be famed for something is a fairly formal alternative to be famous for.

items.example: Researchers are studying the factors that influence longevity.
items.note: A long life or long duration, depending on context.

items.example: The athlete hopes to attain a personal best this season.
items.note: Fairly formal synonym for reach or achieve, particularly a level or goal.

items.pt: expectativa de duração da vida; tempo de vida
items.example: Better nutrition can increase an animal's average lifespan.
items.note: How long a person, creature or product lives or lasts.

items.example: The volunteers tend the injured animals every morning.
items.note: Tend someone or something means look after; distinct from tend to do something meaning usually do it.

items.example: Some animals hibernate through the winter.
items.note: Enter a state of low activity during colder months.

items.example: Wildflowers grow across the meadow in spring.
items.note: An area of grassland, often used for hay or grazing.

items.example: A buzzard circled above the fields.
items.note: In British English, a type of bird of prey.

items.example: We watched an eagle soar above the valley.
items.note: Fly high or rise without frequent wing movements; also figurative for increases.

items.example: The riverbank is home to a small population of water voles.
items.note: A small semiaquatic rodent, not a bird or fish.

items.example: Conservationists warned of the threat of extinction.
items.note: A risk that a species will disappear entirely.

items.example: The sculptor shaped the stone using a chisel.
items.note: A tool with a sharp cutting edge, often struck with a hammer.

items.example: The waiter brought a large tureen to the table.
items.note: A deep serving dish, traditionally for soup.

items.example: The children clambered over the rocks.
items.note: Climb using hands and feet, usually with effort or awkward movements.

items.example: I get ratty when I have not slept enough.
items.note: Informal, especially British English, for irritable or bad-tempered.

items.example: They offer sugar-free drinks at the cafe.
items.note: The suffix-like second element -free indicates without something.

items.example: Our neighbour is a warm-hearted person who helps everyone.
items.note: A compound adjective meaning kind and caring.

items.word: up to my eyes in work
items.pt: atolado de trabalho; cheio de trabalho
items.example: I'm up to my eyes in work this week.
items.note: Informal idiom: extremely busy with a large amount of work; the possessive changes with the speaker.

items.example: We rented a flat on a tree-lined avenue.
items.note: Compound adjective for a street or road with trees along its sides.

items.example: A cement mixer was operating beside the new building.
items.note: A machine for mixing cement with other materials and water.

items.pt: cartão de crédito de loja; cartão de loja
items.example: The shop offered a discount to customers using its store card.
items.note: A card associated with one retailer or retail group; terms vary by scheme.

items.section: G · Prefixes and word structure exercises
items.example: Please redirect the parcel to my office.
items.note: Re- can indicate doing something again or in a different direction.

items.section: G · Prefixes and word structure exercises
items.example: The child burst into uncontrollable laughter.
items.note: Un- means not; -able relates to possibility.

items.section: G · Prefixes and word structure exercises
items.example: We met for pre-dinner drinks at six.
items.note: Pre- means before, as in pre-dinner or pre-meeting.

items.section: G · Prefixes and word structure exercises
items.example: The journal publishes a bimonthly update.
items.note: Ambiguous: can mean twice a month OR every two months; clarify the intended schedule. Also written bimonthly.

items.section: G · Prefixes and word structure exercises
items.example: I still exchange messages with my ex-boss.
items.note: Ex- marks a former role or relationship.

items.section: G · Prefixes and word structure exercises
items.example: Residents protested against anti-tourist slogans.
items.note: Anti- indicates opposition to or hostility towards something.

items.section: G · Prefixes and word structure exercises
items.example: Disconnect the charger before opening the device.
items.note: Dis- indicates reversal, separation or removal in this verb.

items.section: G · Prefixes and word structure exercises
items.example: Several undelivered letters were returned to the post office.
items.note: Un- creates the negative meaning: not delivered.
